title: Tearing chest pain and a wide mediastinum
subtitle: A 52-year-old man brought to the CTICU from the emergency department with hypertension, tearing chest pain radiating to the back, and a CT angiogram on its way.
objectives: Start anti-impulse therapy before the diagnosis is confirmed, sequence rate control before pressure control, and explain the physiology that justifies the order.
Perform and document the examination that changes management in suspected acute aortic syndrome: pulse deficits, focal neurology, aortic regurgitation, and tamponade.
Build the differential for hypotension in type A dissection and explain why tamponade in this setting is managed differently from tamponade of any other cause.

Receive a handoff after hemiarch replacement under hypothermic circulatory arrest and anticipate the postoperative problems: coagulopathy, neurologic injury, spinal cord and visceral malperfusion, and renal failure.
Recognize late malperfusion from the residual false lumen and know who to call and what imaging and endovascular options exist.

stages.title: Presentation
stages.narrative:
A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension and no other history is transferred to the CTICU from the emergency department because the hospital's dissection pathway routes suspected acute aortic syndrome here while imaging is arranged. [NMH protocol, insert] He describes abrupt, severe, tearing chest pain that began two hours ago and radiates to the interscapular region. The chest radiograph in the ED showed a widened mediastinum. A CT angiogram of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis has been ordered and the scanner will be free in about 20 minutes. [REVIEW]

He is anxious and in pain. Heart rate is in the low 100s, blood pressure in the right arm is markedly elevated, and the ED has not yet measured the left arm. He has a right radial arterial line placed in the ED. Oxygen saturation is normal. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with LV hypertrophy and no ST elevation. Troponin is not yet back. [REVIEW]

The ED gave a single dose of IV opioid and nothing else. The ED resident asks whether to give heparin for a possible coronary syndrome. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Before the CT: commit to what you give, in what order, and to what targets. Then say what you examine in the next five minutes and what you tell the ED resident about heparin.
questions.modelAnswer:
**What you give and in what order.** Anti-impulse therapy, started now, not after the CT. The goal is to reduce the force of LV ejection (dP/dt) and the pressure in the aorta, because both propagate the dissection and both drive rupture. The 2022 ACC/AHA aortic disease guideline recommends intravenous beta blockade as the initial therapy, with a vasodilator added only if the blood pressure remains above target once the heart rate is controlled. [REVIEW] The order matters: a vasodilator given first produces reflex tachycardia and a rise in dP/dt, which is the opposite of what you want. The guideline targets, as summarized in the ACC key points, are a heart rate of 60 to 80 beats per minute and a systolic blood pressure below 120 mmHg, or the lowest pressure that maintains end-organ perfusion (Isselbacher and colleagues, Circulation 2022). [VERIFY] The agent at NMH is likely esmolol, because it is titratable and its short half-life means a mistake can be undone in minutes, with labetalol as the alternative. Esmolol versus labetalol is argued in the controversies section. If a vasodilator is needed after rate control, the options are nicardipine, clevidipine, or nitroprusside. Nitroprusside has the longest track record and the most toxicity. Doses are left to the unit protocol. [NMH protocol, insert] [VERIFY]

**Pain.** Analgesia is part of anti-impulse therapy. Pain drives catecholamines, which drive heart rate and pressure. Treat it properly.

**What you examine.** Five things, in the time you have:

- **Both arms and both legs.** Blood pressure in both arms. If one is lower, the arterial line should be in the arm with the higher pressure, because a line in an arm whose subclavian is involved will under-read and lead to under-treatment or, worse, to vasopressors for a pressure that is not real. [REVIEW] Palpate femoral, popliteal, and pedal pulses and document them, because the baseline is what tells you tomorrow that something has changed.
- **A focused neurological examination.** Level of consciousness, speech, lateralizing weakness, and lower-extremity motor and sensory function. Carotid involvement produces stroke. Spinal involvement produces paraplegia. Either changes the surgical plan and the conversation with the family, and either can appear between now and the operating room, so the pre-CT examination is the baseline.
- **Aortic regurgitation.** A new diastolic murmur, a wide pulse pressure, or a bedside echo showing a regurgitant jet means the root is involved. Acute severe AR into a non-compliant LV produces pulmonary edema and, importantly, means that aggressive rate control may not be tolerated because the LV depends on a short diastole to limit regurgitant volume. [REVIEW]
- **Tamponade.** Distended neck veins, muffled sounds, pulsus paradoxus, and on bedside echo an effusion with chamber collapse. In this patient with a high pressure none of those are present yet. The fact that the pressure is high is itself reassuring about tamponade and rupture, for now.
- **Abdominal examination and urine output** as the baseline for mesenteric and renal malperfusion.

**What you tell the ED resident about heparin.** No. Not heparin, not antiplatelet therapy beyond what he may already take, and not thrombolysis under any circumstances. The ECG shows no ST elevation, and even if it did, inferior ST elevation in a patient with tearing pain and a wide mediastinum is a dissection involving the right coronary until proven otherwise. Anticoagulating or lysing a dissection converts a contained hematoma into free rupture. This is the single most important thing to say out loud in the first five minutes, because the reflex to treat chest pain as a coronary syndrome is strong and the pathway to the cath lab is fast. [REVIEW]

**Who else to call.** Cardiac surgery now, before the CT. If this is type A he goes to the operating room from the scanner, and the surgeon wants the lead time.

stages.title: New data
stages.narrative:
The CT angiogram shows a Stanford type A dissection with an intimal tear in the ascending aorta just above the sinotubular junction, extending proximally to involve the non-coronary and right coronary sinuses with the right coronary ostium arising from the false lumen, and distally through the arch into the descending thoracic aorta to the level of the renal arteries. The left renal artery arises from the false lumen. There is a small pericardial effusion without CT signs of tamponade. The arch vessels arise from the true lumen. [REVIEW]

On return from the scanner, his heart rate has fallen into the 60s on esmolol and his systolic pressure is now low rather than high. He is more drowsy. The ECG now shows ST elevation in the inferior leads. Bedside echo shows an effusion that is larger than on CT, with right atrial collapse, a dilated non-collapsing IVC, moderate aortic regurgitation, and a poorly contracting inferior wall. [REVIEW]

The cardiac surgeon is on the way in. The operating room will be ready in 40 minutes. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Build the differential for the hypotension and say how you separate the causes at the bedside in the next five minutes. Then commit: do you drain the pericardium, and what do you do with the esmolol?
questions.modelAnswer:
**The differential.** Four causes, and in this patient at least three of them are present at once.

- **Tamponade.** The effusion has grown, there is RA collapse and a plethoric IVC. Blood is tracking into the pericardium from the dissected root. This is the leading cause and the most immediately lethal.
- **Acute aortic regurgitation.** Moderate on echo, from a dissected root that has unseated the commissures. Acute AR into a stiff hypertensive LV produces a rapid rise in LVEDP, pulmonary edema, and a fall in forward output.
- **Right coronary involvement with RV and inferior infarction.** The ostium arises from the false lumen, there is inferior ST elevation, and the inferior wall is not moving. An ischemic RV is preload-dependent and poorly tolerant of tamponade or of rate control.
- **Rupture.** Free rupture into the pleura or mediastinum. On the CT there was no hemothorax, but the CT is 20 minutes old. A new large effusion on a repeat bedside ultrasound of the chest, or an abrupt fall in hemoglobin, points here.

**Separating them at the bedside.** The echo has done most of the work. The questions it leaves are the size of the LV (small and under-filled points to tamponade or RV failure, large and poorly contracting points to AR and ischemia), the RV (dilated with poor free-wall motion points to RV infarct), and whether there is new pleural fluid. A rapid hemoglobin tells you about rupture. The ECG has already told you about the RCA.

**The esmolol.** Reduce it or stop it. The target of 60 to 80 beats per minute was set for a hypertensive patient whose problem was propagation. He is now a hypotensive patient with tamponade, AR, and an ischemic RV, and all three are rate-dependent. In tamponade, stroke volume is fixed and output depends on rate. In acute AR, a longer diastole means more regurgitant volume. In RV ischemia, bradycardia is poorly tolerated. The esmolol was correct an hour ago and is wrong now, and the short half-life is exactly why it was chosen. Do not replace it with a vasopressor reflexively. A modest dose of a vasopressor to maintain coronary perfusion pressure while the pericardium and the root are being dealt with surgically is reasonable. Inotropes raise dP/dt and are a last resort. Volume: a small bolus can help tamponade and RV ischemia but will worsen the AR-driven pulmonary edema, so give it in small aliquots with the echo on. [REVIEW]

**Do you drain the pericardium?** This is the counterintuitive part of type A dissection. In tamponade of any other cause, pericardiocentesis is the treatment. In type A dissection, the classic teaching, from Isselbacher and colleagues in 1994, is that pericardiocentesis can be fatal: in their small series most patients who were drained died shortly afterward, with the proposed mechanism that restoring the blood pressure re-opens a communication that the tamponade had sealed and converts a contained leak into exsanguination. [VERIFY] [REVIEW] That observation, in a handful of patients, drove decades of teaching that the pericardium is not to be touched before the chest is open.

The current position is more nuanced. Hayashi and colleagues (Circulation 2012) reported controlled pericardial drainage, meaning a pigtail catheter with intermittent withdrawal of only enough blood to raise the systolic pressure to around 90 mmHg, in 18 patients with critical tamponade before surgery, with an in-hospital mortality of 17% and no drainage-related deaths. [REVIEW] The 2014 ESC aortic guideline is quoted by some sources as giving controlled drainage a class IIa recommendation for temporary stabilization, while a 2025 review states that the ESC guidelines give no specific recommendation. [VERIFY] [REVIEW] The 2022 ACC/AHA guideline's position on pericardiocentesis in type A dissection could not be confirmed this session and must be checked against the full text before this case is released. [VERIFY] The 2024 ESC guideline on peripheral arterial and aortic diseases should also be checked. [VERIFY]

**The commitment for this patient.** The operating room is 40 minutes away and the surgeon is coming. He is hypotensive but perfusing, and he is drowsy but rousable. The right answer is to go to the operating room now, not to drain. Pericardial decompression happens on bypass, under direct vision, with the aorta about to be clamped. If he arrests or becomes unresponsive before the surgeon arrives, controlled drainage of the smallest volume that restores a pressure, not a normal pressure, is the bailout. The volume is measured in tens of milliliters, not hundreds, and the catheter stays in with the stopcock closed. Who performs it, and under what conditions, needs to be settled before the night it happens. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]

**OR timing.** Now. Type A dissection with tamponade, coronary involvement, and AR is a surgical emergency in which every hour of delay carries mortality. The intensivist's job is to keep him alive for 40 minutes without doing anything that makes the surgeon's job harder.

questions.prompt: Single best answer. He has inferior ST elevation and an RCA ostium arising from the false lumen. The interventional cardiology fellow offers to take him to the cath lab for an RCA stent before surgery. What is the right response?
questions.modelAnswer:
**Best answer: Decline, and go to the operating room.** The coronary ischemia is a consequence of the dissection, and the surgeon addresses it by resecting the dissected root and reimplanting or bypassing the right coronary. A cath lab detour costs time that a tamponading, regurgitant patient does not have, and catheter manipulation in a dissected root with a false-lumen ostium risks extending the dissection, perforating the false lumen, or stenting into the wrong lumen. [REVIEW] Antiplatelet loading for a stent would also be given to a patient who is about to be heparinized for bypass and who will bleed after circulatory arrest.

Why the alternatives fall short:

- **Stent first, then surgery.** There are case reports of PCI as a bridge in type A dissection with coronary malperfusion when surgery was not immediately available, and in a patient in cardiogenic shock from a massive RV infarct with a long surgical delay it is a defensible rescue. In a patient whose operating room is 40 minutes away it is not.
- **Thrombolysis.** Never, in a known dissection.
- **Surgery after a period of medical stabilization.** There is no stabilization available. The three causes of his hypotension (tamponade, AR, coronary malperfusion) are all corrected only by the operation.

The one thing to communicate to the surgeon is the finding itself, because RCA involvement changes the operation (likely root replacement or coronary bypass in addition to the hemiarch) and the cannulation strategy.

stages.title: Decision point
stages.narrative:
Eight hours later, you receive the patient from the operating room. The handoff from the cardiac anesthesia team: axillary arterial and right atrial cannulation, cooling to moderate hypothermia, hemiarch replacement under hypothermic circulatory arrest with unilateral antegrade cerebral perfusion for a period under 30 minutes, aortic valve resuspension with root reconstruction, and a vein graft to the right coronary artery. The pericardium contained a large volume of old and fresh blood. Separation from bypass required a moderate dose of inotrope and a vasopressor. Bleeding was substantial after protamine and was treated with blood products and a fibrinogen concentrate. Chest tube output on arrival is brisk. [REVIEW]

He is intubated and sedated. Pupils are equal and reactive. Temperature on arrival is low-normal. Bilateral cerebral NIRS values are symmetric and similar to the pre-induction baseline. Arterial pressure is at the low end of acceptable on vasopressor. Lactate is elevated. Urine output since the operation has been low. Hemoglobin is low, platelets are low, INR is elevated, fibrinogen is low-normal after replacement, and a viscoelastic test is pending. [REVIEW]

The residual dissection extends from the distal anastomosis through the descending aorta to the renal arteries, with the left renal artery still supplied by the false lumen. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Set the blood pressure target for tonight and justify it against the competing demands. Then list, in order of what will kill him first, the problems you are watching for over the next 12 hours and how you will detect each.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Blood pressure target.** The pre-operative target (systolic below 120 mmHg, from the 2022 ACC/AHA guideline) was set to limit propagation and rupture of an unrepaired ascending aorta. [VERIFY] That aorta has been replaced. What remains is a residual dissected descending aorta with a patent false lumen, fresh suture lines, a brain that has had circulatory arrest, a spinal cord and left kidney perfused through a dissected aorta, and a coagulopathy. These demands conflict. The suture lines and the residual false lumen argue for a low pressure. The brain, the cord, the kidney, and the gut argue for a higher one. Most centers settle on a mean arterial pressure in the normal range, avoiding both hypertension that stresses the anastomoses and hypotension that under-perfuses the cord and the visceral branches, and accept that the number is a compromise rather than a guideline. [REVIEW] The guideline gives long-term targets for chronic dissection management but the immediate postoperative number is institutional. [NMH protocol, insert] [VERIFY] Two practical points: the arterial line should be in a limb whose supply you trust (the right radial is reasonable after right axillary cannulation only if the cannulation site is healthy, and a femoral line in a dissected aorta may read the false lumen), and the target should be revisited the moment the neurologic examination or the urine output changes. [REVIEW]

**What will kill him first, in order.**

1. **Bleeding.** Brisk chest tube output after circulatory arrest in a patient who was hypothermic, has had a long bypass run, has low platelets and fibrinogen, and whose pericardium was full of blood. The approach is to correct what the viscoelastic test shows (fibrinogen, platelets, factor deficiency, residual heparin), to keep him warm, to keep the pressure from rising, and to set a threshold for return to the operating room with the surgeon before the night starts rather than at 3 a.m. Tamponade can recur from a clot in the pericardium, and on a patient whose chambers are now small and stiff it may show as rising filling pressures with falling output rather than the textbook picture. The threshold for re-exploration and the product strategy are institution-specific. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]
2. **Neurologic injury.** Stroke from embolism or hypoperfusion during arrest, and global injury from the arrest itself. The detection is the examination, which means a sedation strategy that allows a neurologic assessment as early as it is safe, and a low threshold for imaging if the examination is asymmetric or if he does not wake as expected. NIRS asymmetry is a trend signal, not a diagnosis. Temperature management after circulatory arrest (avoiding hyperthermia during rewarming) is a reasonable principle with limited evidence. [REVIEW]
3. **Spinal cord ischemia.** The residual dissection involves the descending aorta and the intercostal supply. Paraplegia can appear hours after the operation, and the detection is a lower-extremity motor examination every time sedation permits. If weakness is found, the response is to raise the mean arterial pressure and to consider lumbar drainage, which is extrapolated from the thoracoabdominal aneurysm and TEVAR literature rather than from dissection trials. [REVIEW]
4. **Renal and mesenteric malperfusion.** The left kidney is on the false lumen. Low urine output tonight is multifactorial (hypothermia, bypass, hypotension, contrast), but a kidney that is not perfused will not recover with volume. Mesenteric ischemia presents late and non-specifically: rising lactate out of proportion to the hemodynamics, abdominal distension, a rising transaminase, and bloody stool. It is the complication most often missed because the patient is sedated and the abdomen is not examined. [REVIEW]
5. **Low cardiac output.** From the RV that was ischemic before the operation, the stunned myocardium, and residual AR if the resuspension is imperfect. Echo on arrival and again if the pressure falls.
6. **Limb ischemia** from the cannulation sites and from the residual dissection. Pulse examination documented against the pre-operative baseline.

**Coagulopathy after circulatory arrest** deserves its own sentence. Deep and moderate hypothermia impair platelet function and the coagulation cascade, the long bypass run consumes factors and activates fibrinolysis, and the pericardial blood has already consumed clotting factors before the operation started. The viscoelastic test is the guide. Empiric product administration without a test is the fallback, not the plan. Antifibrinolytic use is standard. Recombinant activated factor VII and prothrombin complex concentrates are rescue agents with thrombotic risk in a patient with fresh grafts and a false lumen. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]

stages.title: Complication
stages.narrative:
Postoperative day 2. He was extubated on day 1 with a normal neurologic examination and symmetric strength. Bleeding stopped overnight on day 0 after product correction. Urine output recovered. He is on an oral beta blocker and an oral vasodilator with his pressure at target. [REVIEW]

This morning he reports a dull abdominal pain that has been present for several hours and that he did not want to complain about. On examination the abdomen is mildly distended with reduced bowel sounds. His left leg is cooler than the right, the left femoral pulse is weaker than it was on the pre-operative baseline, and he describes the left leg as heavy. Lactate has risen. The surgical team is in the operating room with another case. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: What is happening, who do you call, what imaging do you order, and what are the treatment options? Commit to a sequence.
questions.modelAnswer:
**What is happening.** Dynamic or static malperfusion from the residual false lumen. The repair replaced the ascending aorta and hemiarch, but the dissection flap persists in the descending and abdominal aorta. The true lumen can be compressed by a pressurized false lumen (dynamic obstruction, which varies with pressure and flap position) or a branch vessel can be sheared off into a thrombosing false lumen (static obstruction). The abdominal pain, distension, and rising lactate point to mesenteric malperfusion. The cool, heavy left leg with a diminished femoral pulse points to iliac malperfusion on the same side. Both can be from a single flap that has shifted now that the proximal repair has changed the flow dynamics in the false lumen. This is a surgical and endovascular emergency, and mesenteric ischemia in particular has a mortality that rises by the hour. [REVIEW]

**Who you call.** Three calls, in parallel. The cardiac surgeon who operated, even though they are in another case: they need to know, and the decision about re-intervention belongs to them. Vascular surgery or the aortic endovascular team, because the treatment is likely endovascular and the cardiac surgeon may not be the one doing it. Interventional radiology, if the endovascular aortic program sits there at NMH. The specific team structure is institutional. [NMH protocol, insert]

**Imaging.** A CT angiogram of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with arterial and delayed phases, now. It shows true lumen compression, the origin of each visceral and iliac branch (true or false lumen), the presence of thrombus, and the state of the repair. A bedside Doppler of the left leg can be done while the CT is arranged but should not delay it. A lactate trend, a repeat abdominal examination, and a creatinine are the clinical markers. Do not wait for peritonism. By then the bowel is dead. [REVIEW]

**Treatment options.**

- **Optimize the pressure.** Dynamic obstruction is pressure-dependent. If the true lumen is being collapsed by a hypertensive false lumen, lowering the pressure can help. If the true lumen is under-perfused because the patient is hypotensive, raising the pressure can help. The CT tells you which. This is a temporizing adjustment, not a treatment. [REVIEW]
- **TEVAR.** A stent graft covering the primary entry tear, or the most proximal re-entry in the descending aorta, expands the true lumen and depressurizes the false lumen. It is the treatment for dynamic malperfusion from the descending aorta and is the approach recommended by the 2022 ACC/AHA guideline for complicated type B dissection with malperfusion, which the residual dissection after type A repair now physiologically resembles. [REVIEW] The landing zone after a hemiarch repair may be in the graft, which is a favorable landing zone, or in the native arch, which raises the left subclavian question.
- **Fenestration and branch stenting.** For static obstruction of a single branch (a sheared mesenteric or iliac origin), a stent into the branch from the true lumen, or fenestration of the flap with a balloon or a needle to equalize the lumens, is the targeted approach.
- **Open surgery.** Laparotomy for bowel resection if the gut is already infarcted, and open fenestration or bypass if the endovascular route fails. The mortality is high.

**The sequence.** Call the surgeon and the endovascular team while the CT is being arranged. CT now. Adjust the pressure in the direction the CT indicates. Endovascular treatment within hours. Laparotomy if the lactate does not fall or the abdomen worsens after revascularization, because reperfusion of ischemic bowel does not guarantee viability. Antibiotics for translocation and nil by mouth while this is being decided. [REVIEW]

**The lesson.** The repair of a type A dissection is a repair of the part that kills in the first hours. The residual false lumen is a lifelong problem that can declare itself on day 2 or in year 5, and the examination that detects it is the one the fellow does with their hands.

teachingPoints:
- Anti-impulse therapy starts on suspicion, not on confirmation. Beta blocker first, vasodilator second, with the 2022 ACC/AHA targets of heart rate 60 to 80 and systolic below 120 mmHg or the lowest pressure that perfuses. [VERIFY] A vasodilator given first produces reflex tachycardia and raises dP/dt.
- Esmolol is chosen for its short half-life, which matters in a patient whose hemodynamics can reverse in an hour. Analgesia is part of anti-impulse therapy.
- The examination before the CT (both arms, four limbs, neurologic status, AR, tamponade) is the baseline against which every later change is measured. Put the arterial line in the arm with the higher pressure.
- No heparin, no antiplatelet loading, no thrombolysis. Inferior ST elevation with tearing pain is RCA involvement until the CT says otherwise.
- Hypotension in type A dissection has four causes (tamponade, AR, coronary malperfusion, rupture) and they coexist. The anti-impulse regimen that was right an hour ago may be wrong now.
- Pericardiocentesis in type A tamponade is the exception to the rule. The classic teaching (Isselbacher 1994) is that it kills by re-opening the leak. The modern position is that controlled drainage of tens of milliliters to a systolic around 90 mmHg is a bailout before the operating room, not a treatment. Guideline positions on this are inconsistent and must be checked. [VERIFY]
- RCA involvement is addressed by the surgeon. A cath lab detour costs time and risks the false lumen.
- After circulatory arrest, bleeding and coagulopathy, neurologic injury, spinal cord ischemia, visceral and renal malperfusion, and low output are the sequence to watch. The blood pressure target is a compromise between suture lines and perfusion, and it is institutional.
- The residual false lumen is a lifelong problem. Late malperfusion presents as abdominal pain, a cool limb, or a rising lactate, and the treatment is endovascular (TEVAR, fenestration, branch stenting) and urgent.
pitfalls:
- Waiting for the CT to start anti-impulse therapy.
- Giving a vasodilator before the heart rate is controlled.
- Measuring blood pressure in one arm and treating a number that is falsely low because the subclavian is involved.
- Heparin for a chest pain patient whose mediastinum is wide.
- Continuing a beta blocker at the pre-operative target in a patient who has become hypotensive from tamponade, AR, or RV ischemia.
- Draining the pericardium to a normal blood pressure.
- Accepting a cath lab detour for RCA involvement when the operating room is minutes away.
- A femoral arterial line in a dissected aorta that reads the false lumen.
- Keeping the patient too deeply sedated to examine the legs after circulatory arrest.
- Attributing day-2 abdominal pain to ileus or the incision, and attributing a cool leg to the cannulation site, without a CT.
controversies:
**Esmolol versus labetalol.** Both are supported for initial rate and pressure control. Esmolol is beta-1 selective, ultra-short-acting, titratable, and reversible within minutes, which makes it the preferred agent in a patient whose hemodynamics may reverse. Its costs are the infusion volume at high doses and the need for a separate vasodilator. Labetalol is combined alpha and beta blockade, lowers pressure and rate together, and can be given as boluses or infusion, but it has a long half-life and cannot be quickly undone when the patient tamponades. The guideline does not mandate one over the other. Most dissection pathways in the United States use esmolol first. [REVIEW] [NMH protocol, insert]

**Pericardiocentesis in type A tamponade.** The 1994 Isselbacher series taught a generation that drainage was lethal. The 2012 Hayashi series showed that controlled drainage to a systolic around 90 mmHg could be done safely in critical tamponade before surgery. The 2014 ESC aortic guideline is quoted by some sources as giving controlled drainage a class IIa recommendation for temporary stabilization, while a 2025 review states that the ESC guidelines give no specific recommendation. The 2022 ACC/AHA guideline's wording on this point and the 2024 ESC peripheral arterial and aortic guideline's wording were not confirmed this session. [VERIFY] The practical position most centers hold is that drainage is a bailout for the patient who will not survive to the operating room, that the volume removed is the minimum that produces a pressure, and that the operating room is the treatment. Whether a CTICU should have a controlled drainage protocol at all, and who performs it, is an institutional decision. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]

**Extent of the initial repair.** Hemiarch replacement addresses the ascending aorta and the proximal arch and is the fastest, lowest-risk operation. Total arch replacement, with or without a frozen elephant trunk, addresses arch tears and sets up the descending aorta for later endovascular treatment, at the cost of a longer arrest time and higher operative mortality and stroke risk in most series. The argument for a more extensive initial repair is that it reduces late false lumen expansion and reintervention. The argument against is that the patient has to survive the first operation and that most do not need the second. The 2021 AATS expert consensus on surgical treatment of type A dissection and the 2022 ACC/AHA guideline both frame the decision by the location of the primary tear and by patient and center factors rather than by a single rule. [VERIFY] [REVIEW] This patient's tear was in the ascending aorta and the arch vessels arose from the true lumen, which is the classic hemiarch indication.

**Management of the residual false lumen.** After type A repair, a patent false lumen in the descending aorta is associated with late aneurysmal degeneration and reintervention. Whether to treat it early (TEVAR or frozen elephant trunk at or soon after the index operation), to treat it only when it becomes complicated (malperfusion, rapid growth, rupture), or to treat it based on imaging predictors (false lumen diameter, partial thrombosis, entry tear size) is unresolved. The guideline supports intervention for complicated residual dissection and surveillance for uncomplicated, which is where this patient was until day 2. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

**Antegrade versus retrograde cerebral perfusion, and the temperature of arrest.** Not a decision the intensivist makes, but the handoff should include it because unilateral antegrade perfusion carries a theoretical risk to the contralateral hemisphere if the circle of Willis is incomplete, and the degree of hypothermia changes the coagulopathy and the rewarming plan. [REVIEW]
discussWithAttending: You started esmolol in a hypertensive patient and he tamponaded an hour later. Reconstruct the moment you should have recognized that the regimen needed to change, and say what you would want the bedside nurse to be watching for in every dissection patient on anti-impulse therapy.
Defend the statement that you would never drain the pericardium in a type A dissection. Then describe the patient, the time to the operating room, and the technique with which you would do it anyway.

The pre-operative examination found a weaker left femoral pulse than the right. Does that change the cannulation plan, the arterial line site, or your day-2 interpretation of a cool left leg? What would you have wanted documented?

Set the postoperative blood pressure target for a patient with a fresh hemiarch graft, a residual false lumen to the renals, a brain that has had 25 minutes of circulatory arrest, and a coagulopathy. Then say what number you would accept if he started bleeding, and what number you would accept if he developed leg weakness.

A total arch with frozen elephant trunk would have treated the descending false lumen that caused the day-2 malperfusion. Argue that the surgeon should have done it, then argue that they were right not to.

references.note: Citation confirmed this session. The heart rate target of 60 to 80 and systolic below 120 mmHg (or lowest perfusing pressure), beta blocker first with vasodilator added, immediate repair for type A with malperfusion, and intervention for complicated type B were confirmed via the ACC Ten Points summary of the guideline, not the full text. The guideline's wording on pericardiocentesis in type A tamponade, on postoperative blood pressure targets, and on extent of arch repair could not be confirmed this session and is marked [VERIFY] in the text.
